item.title: The Fight Against Overwork
item.description:
Leadership

The Fight Against Overwork

Champions can help you in your fight against overwork.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Cultures of overwork are harmful and hard to overcome.
  • Making a change to a culture requires others to champion what you are doing.
  • Great leaders know they can't do it all alone.

Employee wellness has recently been deprioritized in many organizations, replaced by a heightened focus on profit and efficiency. While research shows that wellness improves performance, many organizations opt to focus solely on productivity, leaving wellness in the hands of the employees. However, many individual leaders understand the importance of taking care of their people and want to support employee wellness. Because of this philosophical difference, these leaders tend to face a variety of challenges when attempting to implement great practices on their teams. Specifically, these well-meaning leaders often find themselves fighting against cultures of overwork.

Why Fight Cultures of Overwork?

Cultures of overwork are unfortunately easy to find in organizations, especially in the U.S. Many executive teams focus on creating "lean" teams in support of their focus on improved efficiency and productivity while keeping costs down. However, many of these teams are actually understaffed and overworked, with "lean" translating to "starving for support." Cultures of overwork have the opposite impact than they intend, often leading to reduced efficiency, productivity, and performance. Overwork can lead to burnout—for both employees and their leaders. Leader burnout is particularly harmful as it tends to have a trickle-down effect on their employees.

These types of cultures are tricky to overcome. When others believe that time equals productivity, trying to shift away from overwork can make you seem lazy or lacking dedication.

So, what can you do to fight against overwork for your team? You can start with finding champions.

Who Are Your Champions?

Many of the organizations we studied had at least one or two leaders who truly understood the importance of employee wellness. Do you know who those people are?

Ask yourself a couple of key questions to identify those leaders:

  • Whom do people love to work for?
  • Who has a great reputation as a caring leader?
  • Whose team has the highest retention rate?

It never hurts to ask people you trust to help identify leaders who are aligned in your fight against overwork.

Rally Your Champions

Once you’ve identified your possible champions, set up some time with them to talk. An honest conversation between two like-minded people can go a long way in helping you determine how to move forward. Ask if they’d be willing to help you strategize on how to gain support for your efforts in shifting the culture on your team. Check if they’d be willing to join you in your fight against overwork. If they say yes, create recurring meetings and bring in other champions as you find them. There is power in numbers—leverage this new team of overwork fighters to create a plan to support each other and make a case for change in the broader organization.

There are many ways your new group can make a difference. Here are some ideas to get you started:

  • Leverage each other to help hold boundaries for your teams. In other words, if you work cross-functionally, don’t overstep on another person’s boundaries outside of your team. Ask your champions to ensure it doesn’t happen when their team works with your team either.
  • Make a pact to hold your own boundaries. If you all are logging off in the evening or not responding to emails on weekends, it makes it harder for other leaders to blame one person for not “working hard enough." Plus, role modeling good behaviors may inspire others to do the same.
  • In broader meetings with other leaders, support each other when one of you is pushing back on unrealistic deadlines or asking for additional support.
  • Work together to create a plan to prove that wellness doesn’t hurt performance. Think about measurement. What does success look like on your team? Keep track of those metrics and how they change over time as you reduce overwork and implement a more wellness-focused culture.

Work together with your champions and use your creative minds with deep knowledge of your specific organization to find what works best for you in your battle against overwork!

item.title: “That’s So Traumatic!”
item.description:
Social Media

“That’s So Traumatic!”

Why does it seem like clinical language is everywhere in the culture right now?

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Clinical language is expanding into non-clinical settings.
  • Clinical language is being distorted in digital spaces.
  • Young social media users are apt to self-diagnose mental health conditions.

Since the time last week that my adolescent nephew used the term “trauma” in a phone conversation to describe something that happened to him at Washington Square Park, i haven't been able to stop reflecting on how fully clinical language is being embedded in the vernacular among developing youth. While the psychologist (and doting aunt) in me had my antenna up when he used the term, I was also relieved to hear that while what he was describing that happened at the park was distressing for him, it was not, in fact, a description of a traumatic event.

Neuro-atypical. Narcissism. Insecure attachments. Panic attacks. Trauma. It seems like in every corner of the culture, clinical language is being used: Scroll through a young user’s social media feed, and there are bound to be influencers whose usernames or handles have accompanying descriptions seeped in clinician speak—recovery, trauma, inner child, addiction—regardless of whether or not they have actually undergone any kind of mental health evaluation and/or intervention for a given disorder or episode.

In my book, Disconnection: The Search for Identity in a Digital Age, I discuss how many young social media users are deriving a sense of self or identity by overly relying on a diagnosis of a mental health issue—often without such a diagnosis ever having been verified by a credentialed mental health professional (Aalai, 2026). Similarly, last month, psychiatrist Suzanne Garfinkle-Crowell wrote an essay in The New York Times reflecting on how she started to notice a trend several years ago among young women in particular of announcing a self-diagnosis on social media—and, often, on their first visits to her office (Garfinkle-Crowell, 2026). “The patients of this new wave,” she mused, “were talking in therapy-speak, and their therapy hadn’t even started."

Given the role that language plays in serving as a cognitive framework with which we understand and process the world around us, I can’t help thinking: What does it mean that so many developing youths right now are appropriating clinical language in non-clinical settings? On the one hand, the notion of silencing as a form of stigma—say, around acknowledging trauma—appears to be a thing of the past. As someone working in higher educational settings, I can attest that students today are not shy about engaging with topics related to mental health. On the other hand, if everything is traumatic, then nothing is traumatic, and the term “trauma” loses all usefulness. Moreover, there is a chasm between using clinical language the way it is being used in our culture right now versus actually describing personal experiences or interactions that meet the diagnostic standard for a mental health disorder—or even a symptom.

In other words, a lot of students may use the term “traumatic” or “narcissism” when they engage with me during a lecture, but what they are describing often doesn’t match up to the clinical weight of such language. For instance, I was sharing an anecdote about someone seeking me out based on my expertise to ask what it means if a person who made a mistake appears unwilling to apologize, and before I even finished the sentence, a student quipped, “Isn’t that narcissism?”

Labels can be comforting. During a time of volatility in so many dimensions of young people’s lives—politically and economically, to name the most obvious—perhaps the illusion of certainty that comes with a diagnosis of a psychological disorder is appealing precisely because, well, it gives the user some semblance of stability.

Fellow PT contributor Mara Whiteside reflected on this very topic last year, identifying the role exposure to mental health content on TikTok is likely playing in increases of self-diagnoses of such conditions (Whiteside, 2025). One major concern is that there are no guardrails on social media platforms, so the same digital spaces that have become the pipeline for information among developing youth are also purveyors of rampant falsehoods and mis/disinformation.

I don’t yet entirely know what this burgeoning clinical-speak our youth are appropriating means, but what it does allude to is something I think we all need to be sensitive to: All is not well with young people right now, and perhaps clinical-speak is the siren song they are using as a means to get more support/attention from the adults in the room.

item.title: Awake on Purpose: A Practical Guide to Everyday Mindfulness
item.description:
Mindfulness

Awake on Purpose: A Practical Guide to Everyday Mindfulness

Exploring mindfulness and learned mindfulness.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Mindfulness is deliberately noticing one’s impulses, thoughts, behaviors, and reactions.
  • Practicing mindfulness reduces burnout, improves relationships, and eases anxiety and stress.
  • Mindfulness turns frustrating resistance into useful information, focus, making everyday tasks more engaging.
  • Mindful mindedness extends self-observation with empathy and perspective-taking: thought and emotion aligned.

Mindfulness pulls attention away from distraction and competition. It settles a person and eases tension, especially at work. Stepping back changes how we relate to others. Learning mindfulness depends on staying open to feedback. This waking up doesn’t happen once — it repeats as new situations arise. It also depends on genuine closeness with other people, something easy to lose sight of. I offer this as a starting definition: deliberate awareness of our own impulses and behaviors.

Learned Mindfulness is a set of practical guidelines. None of this is new — it draws on traditions that go back centuries (Thich, 1975). It is also a tool I use every day. In therapy, it lowers anxiety and helps people communicate better. Mindful dialogue depends on taking another person’s perspective and feeling empathy—mindful mindedness.

Mindfulness
Source: Artem Podrez, photographer; pexels-artempodrez-6951484.jpg

Awake on Purpose Minimizes Physical and Emotional Exhaustion

Mindful interactions lower the risk of burnout—the felt sense of pushing against life; engagement is the felt sense of moving with it.

With learned mindfulness, people start making better choices about how they live, what they eat, and whether they exercise. Relationships often improve the most. Over time, relationships with others and with our own experience change for the better. Old habits that lead to harmful behaviors can change. So can the anxiety and stress that come with them. This takes practice, but you can learn it.

An example of learning mindfulness came up when a patient described her week. At first, she spoke in a monotonous, hurried voice. She was fidgety and struggled to focus. Her discomfort was transferring to me. As I noticed her behaviors and felt them as uncomfortable, I regrouped and refocused. For example, I tried to pause before answering, to breathe slowly, and to lower my voice. Then she stopped mid-sentence, looked at me directly, and said, “You seem calmer than I feel.”

That was the entire intervention. I hadn’t given her advice. I let her borrow my nervous system, attuned to "equipoise," for a moment. This is what I mean by empathetic, mindful mindedness in clinical work—not a technique applied to the patient, but a state I maintain that the patient can find and use.

Learned Mindfulness is my "emotional-intelligence-and-integrity” approach to mindfulness — an evolving awareness put into practice. Put directly, emotional intelligence, or EI, describes the qualities of someone who functions well psychologically, primarily through mood regulation. Along with a steady mood, equanimity and equipoise are two terms I use for even-minded attention—a level head and perspective applied to “the stuff of everyday life” (Ninivaggi, 2017).

Learning Mindfulness Makes Engaging in Life Enjoyable

Enjoyable activities also benefit from mindfulness. For example, when my mind wanders and I lose focus, I feel resistance. This obstacle is frustrating, if not annoying. Exercise and hobbies, like work tasks, suffer. However, if I notice and engage with these unsettling feelings, that same resistance becomes information. My focus sharpens, and the activity becomes more engaging. The task didn’t get easier; my attention stopped fighting it.

When thought aligns with the natural rhythm of emotion, reasoning improves. Thoughts and emotions reset each other. Perception, however, is never complete. Without sufficient information, confusion follows, leading to stress, bias, and blind spots.

Confused thinking produces cognitive dissonance and ambivalence. As uncertainty accompanies anxiety, it threatens sound decision-making. Stress runs through these thoughts and feelings. Clarity, emotional and conceptual, can wear the body down enough to blunt everyday effectiveness. Mindfulness, as clear perception and emotional lucidity, keeps thinking focused.

“Mindful Mindedness” goes beyond psychological mindedness. It adds empathy and perspective-taking to self-observation, moment by moment. Learned Mindfulness is the method I use to cultivate that capacity.

item.title: Journaling in the AI Era
item.description:
Career

Journaling in the AI Era

How to balance stress management and personal security when keeping a journal.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Regular journaling offers emotional benefits.
  • Digital journals on work devices can become public in legal cases, risking privacy exposure.
  • Handwritten journals offer greater privacy in the AI era and encourage mindful self-reflection.

In this post, we will discuss the value of keeping a journal as well as the challenge of keeping your personal information safe in this emerging AI/quantum computing era.

The Value of Keeping a Journal

Readers may think of diaries or journals as written by adolescent girls who vomit out feelings onto blank sheets. But the act is itself tension-relieving. Looking at those written words days or weeks later can provide cognitive perspective that was impossible to obtain at the time.

Personal journals are not, however, limited to adolescent girls. These are just a few of the famous leaders who kept diaries: John Quincy Adams, Marie Curie, Bob Dylan, Harry Truman, and Ronald Reagan.

Diaries as Stress-Release Mechanisms

In an article about the value of writing journals, Spera et al. (1994) conducted a research project involving 63 high technology employees who were all laid off on the same day. Twenty-one participants wrote a diary every day with their deepest feelings, while 21 kept a daily spreadsheet calendar with no expression of feelings. And 21 participants did nothing.

Three months later, 68 percent of participants who wrote diaries found jobs, while only 48 percent of participants who used spreadsheets and 27 percent of participants in the control group managed to find employment.

There was no significant difference between the three groups in terms of networking meetings, phone calls, or letters sent. The authors suggested that conducting a job search is stressful, and that the inhibition of stressful feelings creates stress about stress, and this meta-stress inhibits success (Spera et al., 1994).

Risk Management in Journal Writing

While writing a daily journal can be beneficial, the location of your written material is an important risk management issue. For example, Greg Brockman, co-founder and president of OpenAI, began writing a diary and saved the files in his business laptop. Former OpenAI investor Elon Musk launched a lawsuit against OpenAI, and Brockman’s laptop was subpoenaed for evidence.

An entry from Brockman’s diary became Exhibit 161 in a public trial. The Wall Street Journal made some of the personal contents public (Cohen, 2026). The combination of computer power and artificial intelligence allowed Musk’s lawyers to comb through the information, finding the revealing entry.

Former NIAID Director Anthony Fauci is another prominent journal keeper. During the Covid-19 pandemic, Fauci served under President Trump as a lead member of the Coronavirus Task Force. He later served as President Biden’s chief medical officer. Fauci wrote more than 1,100 pages in his journal, which was kept on his workplace computer.

Years after he left federal employment, copies of his files remained within the NIH and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. The IT department downloaded Fauci’s files and gave them to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., who passed the files to U.S. Senator Rand Paul, a long-time adversary of Fauci. The details of his diary have been leaked to the press (Stolberg, 2026).

Old-Fashioned Becomes State-of-the-Art

In an AI world, the least risky thing may be to write your diary into a basic composition notebook, available for $2.20 online. Keep the notebook in a secure location at home. In addition to the added security, slowing down to deliberately write your thoughts can be emotionally useful.

If You Must Write Your Journal on a Computer

It's best to use a personal computer or laptop that is not connected to your employer. We recommend storing your personal files in a personal cloud account with a well-known company like Apple, Google, Microsoft, or Amazon. These large companies spend the money to make it more difficult for hackers to break in.

Files residing on your personal computer at home may provide easier access for hackers. Do not keep diary files on work-related computers, including laptops provided by your company.

Summary and Conclusions

Vomiting out your stress onto a sheet of paper or a computer screen can be healthy, yet in our emerging AI world, anything digital risks being read by others.

We believe in the psychological value of writing journals. And we believe in the importance of risk management.

item.title: Some Monsters Don't Have Bodies
item.description:
Grief

Some Monsters Don't Have Bodies

Fighting a supervillain might be easier than fighting grief.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Grief, loneliness, and trauma require adaptation rather than a solution.
  • Small actions can restore a sense of agency when situations cannot be changed.
  • Moving forward means learning to integrate painful experiences.
Aunt May and Peter Parker
Source: Sony Pictures

In preparation for the release of Avengers: Doomsday this December, I've been doing my homework. Or, more accurately, I've given myself an excellent excuse to rewatch key movies and television shows from the Marvel Cinematic Universe.

This past July, while watching Spider-Man: Brand New Day, I found myself thinking about something other than Doctor Doom. I started thinking about how much easier it must be to fight a supervillain. Not easy, physically, but psychologically there is something appealing about having an enemy you can see.

Peter Parker can fight villains, but what does he do with the loneliness of living in a world where the people he loves no longer remember him? Wanda Maximoff can move objects with her mind, alter reality, and nearly defeat Thanos single-handedly, but none of those powers allow her to undo the losses of her parents, her brother, or her partner, Vision. There is no Infinity Stone for grief.

Wanda Maximoff
Source: Disney

Perhaps that is one reason these stories resonate so deeply: Eventually, nearly all of us encounter something we desperately want to fight but cannot defeat in the conventional sense.

When There Is Nothing to Punch

Psychologists distinguish between different forms of coping. Problem-focused coping involves trying to change the thing causing our distress. If I'm overwhelmed because I have too much work, I can reorganize my schedule, delegate something, or finish the task. There is a problem, and I can take action against it. That feels good.

Human beings generally like agency. We like believing that our actions can influence what happens next, but many of life's hardest experiences don't cooperate. These experiences often require more emotion-focused coping—not eliminating the source of the pain, but learning how to experience, regulate, understand, and eventually integrate the emotions surrounding it. That's an entirely different kind of fight. In fact, "fight" may be the wrong word choice entirely.

The Seduction of the Villain

A clearly defined enemy provides something psychologically valuable: a target for action. If the problem is Ultron, Thanos, or Doctor Doom, the question becomes: What are we going to do about him?

Grief, however, asks a much more unsettling question: How am I going to live now that this happened? Loneliness asks: How do I build connection when I can't force another person to connect with me? Trauma may ask: How do I feel safe again when my experience has taught me that the world isn't always safe?

Those questions are harder partly because they contain uncertainty and limited control. When we cannot control the thing causing our pain, we sometimes search for something we can control. We work more, avoid reminders, stay constantly busy, replay conversations, and try to solve emotions intellectually. We may also become angry, withdraw, or tell ourselves we should be "over it" by now. Sometimes we even find another problem to fight because fighting something feels better than sitting beside something we cannot fix.

Maybe the Goal Isn't Winning

This may be where superhero stories occasionally teach us something unexpected. Some experiences aren't conquered but integrated. Grief research, for example, does not support the popular notion that everyone neatly progresses through five stages and emerges finished. Grieving is highly individual, and there isn't a prescribed timetable for completing it as our relationship to the loss changes.

Trauma recovery can work similarly. Healing doesn't necessarily mean erasing what happened. It can mean gradually rebuilding safety, connection, routine, and a sense of agency. Finally, loneliness isn't necessarily solved by simply putting more people around us. What we are often seeking is meaningful connection and belonging.

So what do we do when the monster doesn't have a body?

1. Identify what is actually controllable. When something enormous feels uncontrollable, shrink it. You may not be able to answer, "How will I live without this person?” but you may be able to answer, "What do I need today?" You cannot guarantee that you'll never feel lonely again, but you can text one person. You cannot erase a traumatic experience, but you can choose one thing that helps your nervous system feel safer right now.

2. Stop requiring yourself to defeat the feeling. We often make painful emotions worse by deciding their continued presence means we're doing something wrong. Emotions are information and experiences, not opponents. Instead of trying to get rid of a feeling, consider the question of What is this telling me that I need?

3. Resist isolation. Pain often tells us to withdraw at exactly the moment connection matters most, but social support is one of the most consistent resources associated with coping after loss and traumatic experiences. That doesn't mean you have to tell everyone everything. It may mean identifying one or two people with whom you don't have to pretend. Sitting beside someone, going for a walk, watching a movie together, or exchanging ridiculous memes qualifies as connection even if there's no profound conversation involved.

4. Give the experience somewhere to go. Talk about it. Write about it. Make something. Move your body. Create a ritual. Tell stories about the person you lost. The goal is to allow an experience to become part of your story rather than something you must continually outrun.

5. Know when you need another Avenger. Superheroes almost never save the world entirely alone. Neither do humans. If grief, loneliness, or the effects of trauma are significantly interfering with your relationships, work, sleep, or ability to function, professional support can help. It can actually be the most agentic move available.

The Battles Without Final Scenes

Maybe that's what I've been noticing as I work my way through Marvel again. The battles depicted feature impossible odds and heroes getting back up after being knocked down. But the more memorable battles may be the more recognizable ones. Peter Parker standing alone, Wanda trying to construct a life around unbearable absence, and Thor carrying losses that even a god cannot easily manage. Heroes, like us, discover that power doesn't protect anyone from being human.

In December, the Avengers will face Doctor Doom. There will be an enemy and a threat: something to fight. That may be comforting because outside the theater, some of the hardest things we face won't announce themselves with dramatic music.

item.title: Instant Charisma: Increase Your Attraction Quotient
item.description:
Charisma

Instant Charisma: Increase Your Attraction Quotient

Even if you're shy, it's easier to connect with others than you ever imagined.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Noticing others' strengths boosts connection and personal charisma.
  • Everyday actions reveal hidden personal strengths—recognize and appreciate them.
  • Practicing strength-spotting can transform how you listen to and bond with people.

In workshops over the past 10 years, I have taught individuals how to recognize their own strengths. I accomplish this by having each person tell the story of the obstacles and challenges they needed to overcome in order to come to the workshop, such as arranging for time off or getting someone to take care of the kids or the dog, etc. That simple story reveals character strengths that are often ignored or simply taken for granted.

Source: Alexandre Lecocq/Unsplash

Right now, for example, let's use the story of how you made time to read this blog. You might think, "Well, that's no big deal," but it may just uncover strengths you never considered.

So right now, either write down or mentally think of all the steps you took so that you could read this blog. Did you get dressed first? Include that in your story. Did you make a cup of coffee or have a snack to enjoy while reading? Where did you read? Did you make space somewhere in your house or office? Did you leave quiet time so you could read in peace?

Now, let's look at your hidden strengths. First of all, just by taking an interest in this blog, you displayed the strengths of curiosity, love of learning, and initiative!

Then, when you got dressed, you showed the strengths of action and decision-making and appreciation necessary to pick out the clothes that you find beautiful and pleasing. Even the acts of brushing your teeth, showering, and getting dressed are highly underrated—and yet they show the strengths of self-esteem, self-care, and planning.

Let's count enjoying that satisfying cup of coffee or snack as both the strength of self-care and gratitude for the good things in your life.

Lastly, by making space and quiet time to read the blog, you engaged the strengths of wisdom and boundary-setting. Also consider why you are reading this blog and others like it. If you are seeking to learn more about yourself or become a better person for those in your life, then you are showing the strengths of love, humility, self-growth, and broadened perspectives.

When you think about it, even something as seemingly insignificant as remembering where you put your favorite mug or coffee cup displays the strength of memory.

But you may be asking, "What do strengths have to do with charisma and attracting others?" Great question!

I should mention that after I talk about strengths in my workshops, I have people pair up with someone new. Each person then shares an ordinary story. Their partner, meanwhile, listens for the strengths in that story—without interrupting. After hearing the story, the partner reflects back the strengths that they identified in that story. After both have finished telling their stories and having a partner identify their strengths, I ask them this question:

"What was it like to meet someone through the lens of strengths?"

If it were possible to measure the level of goodwill and energy in the room after this exercise, it would be off the charts. Here's what I discovered:

Noticing the strengths of another is a powerful connecting tool that makes people take notice of you. It creates an instant bond.

Basically, noticing another's strengths accomplishes three things.

  1. People feel heard and validated.
  2. Individuals feel safe, and with safety comes a secure attachment and connection.
  3. Individuals feel they are not being judged, and can thus be more authentic and real.

Noticing Others' Strengths Is the Magic Elixir of Connection

Listening for the strengths of others also transforms how you listen. Here's how to do this:

  • Set the intention to notice the strengths of another.

This changes how you engage in any relationship. From the beginning, you are primed for hearing strengths. This opens you up to a fresh way of seeing and being with others. To do this, you'll also need to practice not interrupting the other person. Just listen and let them share.

  • Get in the habit of identifying and naming strengths.

If someone shares a funny story, that's the strength of humor. If someone is caring or thoughtful for another, that's the strength of kindness and compassion; if someone walks the dog, that's the strength of kindness; if someone is good at a task, that's the strength of discipline and mastery.

It can be useful to start by identifying your own strengths. Many different strengths have been named and studied. As a fun exercise, how many can you name and write down?

  • Share Others' Strengths

Let others know about strengths you notice. You can do this right in the moment, and it doesn't have to be obvious. It can be a simple statement such as, "I noticed how that [name strength here] made a difference," or, "How you acted with [name strength here] really is a wonderful coping skill. How did you learn that?"

When you let others share their story and recognize their strengths, you may be surprised how they open up. And, they will appreciate hearing your thoughtful and kind words.

Conclusion

I like to think of sharing strengths as a form of altruism and generosity. It represents a generosity of spirit and a gift that you're offering to another. As another resource, my book Simply Mindful Resilience contains over 100 tools designed to build personal strengths of all kinds.

To get started, make this an everyday practice and enjoy sharing strengths to build relationships in the coming days. What a wonderful way to learn about others, put your own strengths into action, increase your attraction quotient, and celebrate goodwill toward all.

item.title: Being Your Own Person Is a Lot Harder Than It Should Be
item.description:
Conformity

Being Your Own Person Is a Lot Harder Than It Should Be

If it feels like others don't want you to be an individual, you're not wrong.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Trying to be your own person in a world that emphasizes conformity can lead to emotional distress.
  • In today's society, uniqueness may be emphasized, but it is conformity that is actually encouraged.
  • People may be subconsciously motivated to cause difficulties for others trying to be their own person.
  • Being a true individual means questioning what is driving your actions.

In a world that preaches individuality, it is surprising to see how much conformity actually exists. Being a truly different individual takes a lot of conscious effort.

Psychotherapists talk about the concept of cognitive dissonance. This psychological concept relies on the fact that people want very much to believe that what they are doing must be the right thing to do. It is essentially a person falling into a cognitive trap of rationalizing, thinking, “Because I am doing something this way, that must mean it is right.”

We all live in a world where we do not like to admit that we are pretty much making it up as we go along.

Cognitive dissonance affects how people treat other people because if we see people acting differently, then our reaction is often to assume they are wrong. This leads people to live in a world where “different means wrong.” From a deeper perspective, cognitive dissonance is actually the person saying:

  • “If they act, think, or believe differently than me, that means I am wrong.”
  • “And I cannot admit that I am wrong.”
  • “So, either they’re wrong, or I’m wrong.”
  • “And I’m going to choose to say they are wrong.”

It is interesting to see how little the concept of uniqueness fits within this world. Being your own person is really tough. We are all pressured to dress a certain way, think a certain way, and act a certain way. But it is not even that superficial. As human beings, we are also treated in very negative ways if our sense of meaning and purpose does not fit what other people in our social group think is important.

This emphasis on conformity often leads people to one of two different extremes. It can lead to the person feeling that they have to totally conform, not only to what other people they know and see do, but also to the belief systems that other people hold. Or it can lead to another extreme, where everything the person does seems to be in rebellion against what other people believe.

As the existential philosopher Søren Kierkegaard said, becoming an individual is only authentic when the person is not impacted by the crowd in terms of what the person believes, values, or does. It can be useful to keep in mind his famous saying that “the crowd is untruth” as a way of reflecting that anything a person does simply to follow the crowd keeps that person from being a true individual. This applies whether it is following the crowd in terms of determining what to do and what to believe or following the crowd in terms of determining what not to do or believe.

In the field of comparative psychology, which addresses behavior across human and nonhuman animals, behavioral ecologist Rose Trappes (2022) emphasizes how much modern science has lost the idea of true individuality within the social environment and how much uniqueness is actually ignored at the expense of seeing how individual members of a species are affected, either positively or negatively, by what goes on with others.

It is not only the general public that has lost grasp on what it means to be a true individual. Science has lost that as well.

What all this shows is that it can be very difficult to live a life where you are not impacted by the behavior of others, whether it means feeling that you need to act, think, believe, and feel the same way they do or that you need to act, think, believe, and feel the complete opposite of what they do. Functioning in the world where you are working against what people say or do can be equally problematic on a psychological level as simply being like they are.

When functioning within a social group, it is important to think at each step, whenever you can, “What is impacting me here?” “Am I going by what I truly believe is right, or am I going with what I think other people are thinking and doing and then just acting in response to it?”

It is important to keep in mind the question: “Is my behavior based on what I believe, or am I simply functioning as a response to what other people say and do?”

Even if you fully incorporate what other people say and do but have processed it on a level where you believe that what they are saying and doing is right, not because they believe it but because you believe it, then it becomes useful. That extra step is very important.

And if all this seems tough, it is. Keep in mind that being a truly unique individual in a world that really does not value uniqueness or even welcome it as much as it seems to can be a very difficult step. But something being difficult does not mean it is unimportant.

Just because you are different does not mean you are wrong.

item.title: 3 Genius Ways Smart People Deal With Toxic People
item.description:
Forgiveness

3 Genius Ways Smart People Deal With Toxic People

How to deal with toxic people and come out of the encounter happier than you were before it.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Ruminating on toxic people triggers fight-or-flight and steals focus from those you love.
  • You become what you think about, so resenting someone can make you act just like them.
  • There are steps emotionally intelligent people take so toxic people don't live rent-free in their heads.

I've taught emotional intelligence for more than 20 years at Stanford and Yale, written two books on the subject, and given countless keynotes on the topic. No matter what my audience, I always hear the same question:

How do I deal with the toxic people in my life?

After all, everyone has a difficult person: the coworker who undermines you in meetings, the relative who can't resist a jab, or the friend who leaves you feeling small every time you hang up the phone.

The problem is that you find yourself thinking about them way too much. It's like they've moved into your head rent-free, and it feels awful.

Although you'd hate to admit it, you probably think more about the toxic people in your life than the ones you actually love! A snide comment from three days ago replays on a loop while you're trying to enjoy dinner with your family.

It's crazy when you think about it. Here's why and what you can do to help yourself.

Why They Take Up So Much Space

When someone treats you badly, your nervous system reacts as if you're facing a threat. It activates the same fight-or-flight response that would fire if someone were physically hurting you: a flood of stress hormones, a racing heart, a mind that won't let go of the problem.

After all, neuroscience shows that the emotional pain of rejection, for example, activates similar regions of the brain as physical pain. To top it off, the brain tends to focus more on the negative than the positive.

And the fight-or-flight system often does not know the difference between an active threat and a memory of one. Research on rumination shows that replaying a stressful encounter keeps cortisol elevated long after the encounter itself is over. Researchers call this the perseverative cognition hypothesis—i.e. thinking about someone you consider a jerk is, physiologically, almost as stressful as the original interaction. Except now you're doing it to yourself, on repeat, for free.

Step One: Awareness

Here's the biggest problem: If you spend your mental life marinating in anger, suspicion, and resentment toward someone, you unfortunately train your own brain to spin in that cycle. In other words, you turn your bad feelings into a habit.

You may have noticed a very weird phenomenon: Over time, people who despise someone can slowly start to become like the people they don't like. They've spent so many years dwelling on them!

You don't want to become like the person who's bothering you. That's the first step: becoming aware that your anger at someone else's negativity is making you negative. So now what?

Step Two: Forgiveness (This One's for You)

The most well-researched, most effective first step to freeing yourself from negativity is forgiveness.

This isn't about excusing bad behavior or telling the person what they did was fine. Forgiveness, as researchers define it, is letting go of the grip that resentment has on you.

In a classic study, Charlotte Witvliet and colleagues had participants imagine either holding a grudge or genuinely forgiving someone who'd wronged them. Imagining not forgiving someone raised their stress response: heart rate, blood pressure, and sweat gland activity. Imagining forgiveness did the opposite: it calmed all of it back down.

Stanford's Fred Luskin has spent decades studying this in real-world settings. In one randomized trial, a short forgiveness training program significantly reduced participants' perceived stress and trait anger. In another, forgiveness training lowered blood pressure in people with hypertension who ran high on anger. Letting go of a grudge isn't just a metaphor for feeling lighter; it actually shows up on a blood pressure cuff.

You don't have to be friends with this person. You don't even have to be friendly. Forgiveness isn't about them at all. It's about refusing to let their behavior dictate your physiology.

Step Three: Benevolence (Again, for You)

Here's the part most people skip, because it sounds counterintuitive and even unfair. But research suggests it works even better than forgiveness alone: actively wishing the person well. Before you punch the screen, bear with me and look at the research.

Studies show that compassion is actually incredibly healing for you, predicting better mental health, physical health, and even longevity. What's more, it can help you have highly successful relationships.

This is the essence of loving-kindness meditation, a practice with roots in Buddhist psychology that's now been studied extensively in labs. In my own research with colleagues at Stanford, we found that even brief practice generating goodwill toward others shifts people toward more positive emotion and greater social connectedness, benefits that compound over time. Even making you magnetic.

The effects go deeper than mood. In a well-known study by Pace, Negi, and colleagues at Emory, people who practiced more compassion meditation showed lower levels of interleukin-6 (IL-6), an inflammatory marker, in response to a stressful task. Chronic inflammation is linked to everything from heart disease to depression, so wishing someone well isn't just a nice sentiment. It may be doing measurable work inside your body.

If it feels hard to forgive someone and impossible to actually wish them well, consider this: If someone is acting toxic, selfish, mean, or jealous, it's rarely about you. It's usually a sign that they're miserable, insecure, or so lost that manipulation and cruelty are the only tools they know how to reach for. That, of course, doesn't excuse their behavior. But it can help you remember they are deeply unhappy, which can help remind you of compassion.

The Goal Isn't Peace With Them. It's Peace for You.

You don't owe this person closeness. You don't owe them a relationship. What you owe yourself is not becoming toxic in return. This point is important. It's why I've written a whole book about how to have more sovereign relationships.

Forgive first, because it frees you. Then, if you can, wish them well. Because the research is clear: Compassion frees you even further, quiets your nervous system, and may even lower the inflammation running through your body.

Do this, and something interesting happens: The person stops living rent-free in your head—and you get your happiness back, maybe even more than you had before.

item.title: Generative AI and Moral Injury
item.description:
Moral Injury

Generative AI and Moral Injury

Are employers asking workers to betray their values in using AI tools?

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Generative AI tools are supposed to increase employee efficiency.
  • There are limits to how much companies demand that employees sacrifice for efficiency.
  • Asking workers to use AI might put them in a position of having to betray their values.
  • Are we causing a mild form of moral injury if workers are forced to use AI over their objections?
What if your job asked you to use amphetamines to be productive?
Source: Ewa Urban/Pixabay

Consider a hypothetical scenario: A company asks its employees to take amphetamines in order to increase their productivity. The company makes the case that the drugs can be taken in safe doses that won’t have adverse side effects. Plus, the drugs will make the employees work faster, help them concentrate better, and make them more creative and efficient.

Most of us would likely balk at the idea. The employees might reasonably doubt that the dosing is actually safe or that it won’t have long-term effects, despite the company’s claims. Even if the dosing was safe, employees could object that the company shouldn’t ask them to take mind-altering drugs in the name of efficiency. They might also object that using drugs is wrong or that it’s against their values or principles.

The arguments that the hypothetical company makes in favor of amphetamines are similar to arguments they might make in favor of using generative AI. Generative AI can increase productivity by decreasing the amount of time that employees spend on certain tasks. It can help them focus on other things that are more important. It can help jumpstart their creativity and make them more efficient. While we might think it’s fine to object to amphetamines, we might be less likely to object to generative AI. Why?

Some people might deny that drugs and generative AI have that much in common. Drugs alter your brain chemistry and have potentially harmful physical side effects; AI is just software. And yet there is research showing that generative AI also alters your brain: Several studies suggest that using LLMs weaken our cognitive abilities—what is sometimes called "cognitive debt” or “cognitive offloading.” There is also research showing that generative AI use worsens the negative effects of increased screen time, such as isolation, anxiety, and depression.

People might argue that generative AI is just another tool, similar to spreadsheets or email, but that’s not how it’s marketed or how it’s presented by employers. The rhetoric around generative AI is all about how it supercharges employees to be more efficient. But, as the hypothetical case of microdosing amphetamines shows, there can and should be limits to how much we demand that workers do what they can to be more efficient. What if employees have objections to using generative AI tools? Do they feel empowered to resist?

Psychologist Jonathan Shay introduced the concept of moral injury based on his work with military veterans. Moral injury occurs when members of the military are put in situations in which they have to betray their moral values or principles in order to fulfill their professional duties. It would be wrong to compare the moral injury that arises from combat trauma to the moral qualms that people might have using generative AI. The point, though, is that companies might be asking employees to betray their values if they mandate or even encourage generative AI.

People might object to AI tools on a variety of grounds—maybe they are concerned about environmental issues, threats to privacy, or incurring cognitive debt. While we can disagree about how serious these concerns are, they aren’t imagined. Even if microdosing amphetamines was truly safe, employees might reasonably object to taking them just to increase efficiency. They may have similar qualms about generative AI, but it’s not clear that employers are willing to listen.

item.title: Should We Talk About Ariana Grande’s Body?
item.description:
Beauty

Should We Talk About Ariana Grande’s Body?

Perhaps we (or you) could use this moment to start a very important conversation.

Posted September 1, 2026

Co-authored by Heather Widdows, Ph.D., and Jessica Sutherland, University of Warwick

Ariana Grande told People magazine that she is “taking a step back from visibility” because of the “endless, ongoing public scrutiny.” She has had enough of people talking about her body: Is she too thin? Does she have an eating disorder? Is she healthy? Some of the talk about her has been vile. Marina Hyde on The Rest Is Entertainment podcast said the way some people talk about her is “repulsive” and “a massive percentage of it completely without humanity."

But is not talking the answer? When can we talk about other people’s bodies?

Some think "never," because we should not talk about other people’s—especially women’s—bodies. Others think that in Grande’s case we should definitely not speak about her body, as she has repeatedly asked us not to. Others think it’s not that simple. As appearance becomes more valued and valuable than ever before, not to talk about bodies might be failing to talk about something we must talk about. Despite the body positivity movement, everyone wants to be thin. For decades, women have believed that if they could be 10 pounds lighter, they would be happier. Children as young as 3 attach positive characteristics to thinner bodies, and our desire for thinness continues into old age. We routinely put our health at risk to be thin; historically we’ve taken amphetamines and purged; now we diet and exercise and buy black market GLP-1s. In this context, should we really simply not talk about Ariana Grande’s undeniably thin body? Some recognise there is a dilemma here. For example, Emma Madden, who suffered eating disorders herself, writes in The Guardian that “the only honest response may be to acknowledge its contradictions.” This might be true, but acknowledging contradictions isn’t very helpful in practice. We need to know what we can say and what we should say.

Let us start with what we know. We know that body-shaming individuals is harmful. Given this, we should not say negative things about other people’s bodies. It is always body-shaming, and in a world where our bodies are increasingly ourselves, when you shame bodies you shame people. Even when it is supposedly well-intentioned—for example, for health reasons—it can be shaming. Even if it were not shaming (which it is), if someone is overweight or underweight, they almost certainly know this. People know they are too fat or too thin, and usually they are hyper-aware and often feel shame. Key to maintaining an eating disorder is secrecy; pointing out thinness only prompts further withdrawal. It aids the eating disorder. Likewise, pointing out fatness is equally unhelpful. One reason that fat people don’t seek medical help when they need it is they fear, irrespective of why they are seeking medical help, that their weight will be pointed out and they will be shamed. Too often they are right.

The bottom line is that it doesn’t matter who does the shaming—parent, partner, or stranger—and it doesn’t matter why they do it; to be cruel, to inspire, or because they are concerned for the person’s health. The take-home message is that it's best to keep our mouths shut when it comes to saying negative things about bodies. But this doesn’t answer the Grande question. The nasty and negative social media pile-ons are not OK. The trolls know this already. We all know that body shame cuts deep. They do it to be cruel. For whatever reason, we say things online we wouldn’t say in person. And some think celebrities are fair game, as they choose to be in the public eye. But they are also human. So not surprisingly, it is the case that the trolls saying nasty things are wrong to do so; they should shut up.

But there are reasons that we should talk about Grande’s body.

Grande does not want her body talked about, and yet it is. It is being talked about because it is being looked at, and it is being looked at because of her music videos, photoshoots, and appearances. It is legitimate to ask what kind of images of bodies and faces are being held up to us, and to young women particularly, as ideal. The diet of images that we see is remarkably homogenous. Only some bodies are visible, only some bodies are allowed to be seen. Overwhelmingly, the bodies we see are those that conform to the global ideal: bodies that are thin, firm, smooth, and young. Even AI thinks that these bodies are ideal, which tells us exactly what images are out there for AI to learn from. Grande’s body is absolutely conforming, and whether she intends it or not, her body is part of that diet of images that creates an ideal which for most of us, most of our lives, is unattainable. Yet though it is unattainable, we feel ashamed of not having the impossible. It's a constant vicious circle.

We absolutely need to talk about this. We should all talk about bodies much more than we do. What is ideal? Why do we care more about our appearance than our grandparents? Should we? Can we change? How should we relate to our bodies? This includes talking about Grande’s body, however uncomfortable this might be and however horrible for her.

We can feel for her, and we can shame the shamers; trolls should be shamed. But we can’t put the appearance genie back into the bottle by keeping quiet. The scenario in which everyone is looking at her body, but no one dares to speak, is the worst of all possible worlds. Our appearance matters more than ever before, and we must talk about it. There has been far too little conversation about the changing way appearance is valued. Indeed, as a society we have hardly noticed the dramatic difference in how we think about ourselves and our bodies. It is urgent that we think and talk—and talk and talk and talk.

Sorry, Ariana. We get that it’s horrible for you, and we feel for you. But you are not alone. Nearly all of us, especially young women, are in the eye of a destructive storm. Silence will do nothing to help us find our way through. Perhaps we (or you) could use this moment not to withdraw or to shut down comment, but to start a very important conversation?

item.title: A Pattern of Trauma, Dissociation, Rebelliousness, and Shame
item.description:
Dissociation

A Pattern of Trauma, Dissociation, Rebelliousness, and Shame

Trauma can produce dissociated self-states of defiance and self-condemnation.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Rebelliousness may provide a sense of power while causing personal, relational, and occupational consequences.
  • Harsh parenting can foster a submissive identification dissociated from a need to rebel against the parent.
  • Shame intensifies when the consequences of rebelliousness confirm the parent's original negative judgments.
  • Psychodynamic treatment integrates rebellion, self-criticism, and trauma, enabling improved means of coping.

In a prior post (Busch, 2026), I described dissociated representations of self and others (Bromberg, 1998; Busch et al., 2021; Busch, 2024). In these circumstances, individuals in one mode of representation of self and others are unaware of the other mode, disrupting efforts at integration and leading to conflicts within themselves and with others. I wish to describe another form of such dissociative states, in which individuals take pride in rebellion toward authority (or at least what they perceive as authority), leading to adverse consequences and feelings of shame. This rebellion can take several forms, including the use of drugs and alcohol, refusal to properly care for their health, an unwillingness to work in structured occupations, a resistance to sexual or marital mores, or a refusal to follow certain professional or cultural rules, including laws and regulations.

Such individuals often see their rebelliousness as a source of power, and in certain circumstances it can have value. But in many of these instances rebellion takes on a compulsive character, and little thought is given to what consequences there may be for these actions. It can become disruptive of relationships with others, trigger punishment by authorities, lead to poor self-care, and trigger an underlying sense of shame.

The presence of shame is particularly notable, as pride is often expressed about such rebelliousness. Often the shame is triggered when the adverse consequences of the rebellion occur. This can include shame about incidents stemming from intoxication, negative impacts on appearance and health, lack of financial stability, and/or a partner’s anger upon learning of illicit activities.

The exploration of the history of those who evince such dissociated states often reveals an abusive or otherwise traumatizing parent who harshly judges, criticizes, or humiliates the child for perceived inadequacy while setting an impossible standard, or forces compliance through harsh or frightening threats of or actual punishment. A sense of self as rebellious in an effort to express anger and autonomy develops alongside a view of oneself as inadequate and shameful.

The importance of recognizing and integrating these dissociated states is crucial to relieving the problems they cause. It is essential to realize that some of the sense of power in rebellion derives from fighting against an abusive, punitive authority but may be ultimately self-defeating. In addition, it is important to recognize that the sense of shame or assessment of being bad or incapable stems not only from the adverse outcomes of rebellion but from accepting the abusive parent’s viewpoint.

Case Example

John, a 45-year-old single man, presented with depressed and anxious symptoms and described problems with his career and dating. He struggled financially, was supported by his parents, and viewed himself as a “loser.” He believed that women would not be interested in him, based on his lack of financial resources and poor self-care, and had therefore stopped dating. He was actually quite talented in advertising but refused to work “for the man” in a regular advertising agency and depended entirely on freelance jobs. He believed that work in such corporate settings stifled his creativity, and he would rather just live on less money. He refused to exercise because “all the robots out there do it,” and used cannabis on a daily basis. He emphasized that pot spurred his creativity but acknowledged that it reduced his motivation overall and likely added to his increased weight, which he was quite self-critical about. Overall, however, he celebrated his rebelliousness regarding work, exercise, and cannabis use, minimizing the adverse impact of his behaviors.

Exploration revealed that he had a harsh, judgmental father who was highly punitive. He was rigid about the time John needed to spend on his homework, which caused him tremendous boredom. Successful in finance, he did not comprehend John’s writing capabilities and viewed them as meaningless. He called his son a “loser” and disparaged him for not meeting his standards of masculinity, referring to him as a “weakling” or “sissy.” John’s efforts to rebel against these strictures were met with harsh punishment, including his father hitting him with a belt on the buttocks to the point of bruising and long periods of being grounded. As an adolescent, John began to smoke pot and procrastinated on his homework, which lowered his grades and ultimately limited his choice of colleges.

A key aspect of treatment was helping John to recognize that although he purportedly enjoyed his rebellion, these attitudes and behaviors were causing him significant damage. Indeed, he was quite ashamed about his struggles and felt deeply self-critical about what he saw as his “failures” financially and socially. Another step was to help John realize that he had internalized his father’s negative views of himself. Because he was so dissociated from this identification, this information came as a significant shock to him. Indeed, he was for some time unwilling to accept that this could be the case. However, he became increasingly convinced as the therapist continued to point out the similarities between the specific self-attacks he engaged in and his father’s comments about him. For instance, the therapist pointed out John’s references to himself as being a “loser” and “weakling,” terms his father had frequently used to describe him.

With this in mind, the therapist worked with him to revise his perception of his rebelliousness as something to be celebrated and to recognize the damage that he was causing himself. Indeed, he was ultimately acting in accord with his father’s expectations, fulfilling the negative perceptions his father had of him, and accepting his father’s harshly negative views of himself. He slowly began to make efforts to stop using cannabis and regularly exercise. In addition, his increased energy allowed him to seek and take on additional freelance projects, although he still refused to take a regular job. All of these steps aided his self-esteem, enabling him to combat his internalized harsh self-criticisms. Indeed, he resumed online dating, with a belief that women would now be more interested in him. These shifts reduced his symptoms of anxiety and depression.

In this treatment, the therapist was able to identify this pattern of trauma, dissociation, rebelliousness, and shame and eventually help the patient identify these dissociated self and other representations. It is not unusual for this process to take time, as it is difficult to accept both that one is enraged at the traumatizing figure and that one has internalized this figure’s views. A self-punitive element is also part of this cycle, as individuals unconsciously engineer their own self-punishment for their rebelliousness, attacking and damaging themselves. In these circumstances, work within the transference is often valuable, as patients may rebel against aspects of the treatment (e.g., missing sessions) and at the same time fear that the therapist will judge them harshly. This provides a direct in-session opportunity to observe and integrate the dissociative elements.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Seeking to Fulfill Your Career Passion?
item.description:
Career

Seeking to Fulfill Your Career Passion?

Finding a rewarding profession may depend on your attachment style.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Maslow viewed self-actualizing people as dedicated to a calling or social cause.
  • Attachment theory opens a new vista on those who fulfill their career passion.
  • The secure attachment style may be most beneficial for such growth.
  • Secure Attachment Priming (SAP) is proving effective in boosting a secure attachment style.

Do you have a career passion, or are you still looking? Possibly more than ever before, it's a goal emphasized by vocational counselors and, increasingly, their college and even high-school counterparts. In this light, positive psychology uses the term "callings," often signaled by our heady excitement and dedication in discovering a career that feels just right for our soul. Recalling his first, joyful exposure to psychology as a struggling college student, Abraham Maslow likened this exuberant experience to "falling in love" (his words).

As Maslow's biographer, I learned that he regarded career passion as a vital trait of self-actualizers, those thriving at the highest psychological level in his famous hierarchy of inborn needs. In Motivation and Personality, Maslow reported: "They are people who have developed or are developing to the full stature of which they are capable" and are dedicated to a cause or field outside themselves, such as education or the arts, labor organizing, law, medicine, or stay-at-home family caregiving.

Regardless of their specific vocational focus, Maslow insisted in an unpublished essay, self-actualizers have what he called strong "positive human traits" that include the "qualities of self-respect, of security and safety, of being lovable, of being able to love someone else, and of being aware of the need to be loved and to love." These are all emotional-social strengths, of course. But how do these traits actually develop?

Maslow said little on this issue, but shortly before his sudden death at age 62, he planned a guidebook aimed at teens on how to self-actualize. Having raised two daughters to adulthood with his wife, Bertha, and taught college students for over 30 years, he was excited about this ground-breaking project.

Because of Maslow's admiration for such thinkers as Alfred Adler, Anna Freud, and Erich Fromm, it seems likely that this guidebook would have incorporated their ideas. However, a highly relevant body of developmental psychology was still nascent: namely, attachment theory. In my view, it offers vital insights into what helps teens and young adults to self-actualize—and what makes its achievement more challenging and elusive.

Why Attachment Style Matters

Attachment theory is generally traced to the work of John Bowlby, a British developmental psychologist and psychiatrist. In an influential, three-volume work titled Attachment and Loss (1969/1982), he argued that children are born with an innate, biological drive to form a close bond with a primary caregiver, and that the first few years of life comprise a crucial "window" for its formation. The Canadian psychologist Mary Ainsworth amplified attachment theory to emphasize that, based on the subtleties of this crucial bond, we develop an emotional structure that shapes our lifelong ability to become emotionally close with others. Subsequent researchers have broadened attachment theory in recognition of cultural differences in child-rearing practices, but the basic paradigm is that everyone fits one of these four attachment styles: secure, anxious, avoidant-dismissive, avoidant-fearful, or disorganized ( "chaotic").

How does this relate to self-actualization? Simply that without a secure attachment style, it's difficult to enjoy, let alone navigate effectively, the myriad kinds of interpersonal relationships that catalyze our calling. Whether your passion is psychology, health care, or meteorology, you're not likely to gain mentors or develop important collaborative skills—during your college years and afterward—if your attachment style is anxious, avoidant, or disorganized. Studies increasingly show a decisive link between attachment style and workplace relationships, as those with secure attachment evince greater empathy, teamwork, and leadership ability. Such aspects can play a big role in whether you fulfill your career passion.

Boosting Secure Attachment: The Good News

Initially, personality theorists asserted that our attachment style is essentially immutable after childhood. But that viewpoint is now shifting. For example, there's evidence that satisfying life experiences in friendship or love can boost our sense of secure attachment, perhaps permanently. Mounting experimental research also shows that "priming" people with security-oriented images (i.e., a mother hugging her happy child) or guided visualizations (asking participants to picture their favorite place of peace and safety) reduces their attachment anxiety and avoidance. Such activities are called Secure Attachment Priming (SAP).

Another SAP technique is designed to strengthen authenticity. It's based on research that emotionally secure people are less likely to play "head games" with others and are more honest with their feelings. To give it a try, write down all your positive qualities (e.g., kindly, organized) and all your negative ones (e.g., impatient, bossy) each day for a couple of weeks. Give a brief example of each quality. You can vary those from day to day, and be as honest as you can.
